chains.title: Possible NKRF-mediated effect on TERT regulation
chains.element: TERT-associated enhancer annotation; the variant does not overlap the nearby ENCODE cCRE

links.claim: NKRF is the strongest of these binding candidates because its own QBiC-SELEX model predicts a detectable, strong-site preference for ref G. A variant-overlapping NKRF ChIP peak is reported in GM12878, not glioblastoma; the ENCODE query reports no matching-context peak, which may also reflect lack of an experiment. Thus, NKRF occupancy in glioblastoma is unestablished.

The variant has an enhancer regulatory-feature annotation, but it does not overlap an ENCODE cCRE; the nearest pELS cCRE is 75 bp away, and its reported activity scores are maxima across biosamples rather than glioblastoma-specific evidence.

TERT is the nearest listed gene, about 0.5 kb from its TSS, and is among the nearby genes listed for the local cCREs. It is a plausible candidate target, but the evidence does not establish that this element regulates TERT.
Glioblastoma is a proposed context because NKRF is expressed in the reported glioblastoma cell-line panel; expression does not establish occupancy, and the reported overlapping peak is from GM12878.

TERT is relevant to glioblastoma in general, but no evidence here establishes that this variant changes TERT regulation or disease risk. The cited literature's C-allele statement cannot be confidently mapped to the case's G/A alleles.

predictions: If NKRF occupies this site in glioblastoma cells, allele-specific occupancy should favor G over A.
An allele-dependent regulatory effect attributable to NKRF should be reduced by disrupting the NKRF site or depleting NKRF; the direction of any TERT expression change is not established.
falsified_if: Sensitive assays in relevant glioblastoma cells find neither NKRF occupancy nor a reproducible G-versus-A effect.
A reproducible allele-dependent regulatory effect is unchanged by NKRF depletion and disruption of the candidate site.

A major molecular feature of melanoma is abnormal telomerase activation; this is most often caused by telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutations, which occur in 50-82% of cases and are the most common noncoding alteration in this cancer.

Conclusions: Understanding both telomere-dependent and -independent TERT functions is essential for developing effective biomarkers and therapies that overcome resistance and slow melanoma progression.
The genetic landscape of familial melanoma is heterogeneous.
CDKN2A and CDK4 mutations act through UV-dependent and cell cycle disruption pathways, while BAP1, POT1, and TERT mutations are considered UV-independent.
Mutations in the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter region (TPM), particularly C228T and C250T, are common in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (GBM).

The rs[masked] C allele may increase GBM susceptibility and, when in cis with TPM, is associated with reduced TERT expression and poorer prognosis, underscoring its biological and clinical significance in TPM-mutant GBM.
Additionally, loss of either USP10 or FOXM1 suppresses the expression of the downstream target Telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), triggering cellular senescence.

TERT promoter (TERTp) mutations are among the most frequent molecular alterations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type glioblastoma (GBM), yet the molecular profiles and prognostic implications associated with TERTp status remain incompletely characterized.
The prognostic relevance of CDKN2A deletion may vary according to TERTp status, particularly for OS.
